title: Scripts, modules, and how code is loaded
hook: How you load JavaScript changes strict mode, scope, and when code runs. Classic scripts, ES modules, and Node.js `require` versus `import` each have different parsing rules — bundlers hide this until production breaks.

blocks.text: A classic script tag (`<script src="app.js">` without `type="module"`) runs in sloppy mode by default unless `'use strict'` is present, shares the global object for top-level `var`, and executes immediately in document order (blocking parse unless `defer` or `async`). An ES module (`<script type="module">` or `import`/`export` syntax) is always strict, has its own top-level scope (no global `var` pollution), loads with `defer` semantics by default, and supports static `import`/`export` resolved at parse time. Node.js supports both CommonJS (`require`, `module.exports`) and ES modules (`.mjs` or `"type": "module"` in package.json). C# loads assemblies through references — namespaces organize names, but `using` does not load code; `import` in JavaScript actually evaluates and binds the module.

entries.plainDefinition: A file using `import` and `export` with static dependency graph, strict mode, and top-level scope isolation.
Node's original module system using `require()` and `module.exports`. Dynamic, synchronous load.
Using `await` at module top level in ES modules. Pauses module evaluation until the promise settles.

blocks.text: Mixing script types causes subtle bugs: a `var` at module top level is not global, but in a classic script it is. `import` hoisting means dependencies run before your module body — circular imports can leave bindings in the temporal dead zone. Node dual packages (CJS + ESM exports) confuse `default` interop. Bundlers flatten the graph, but Node ESM in production still follows spec rules. C# project references load assemblies at runtime; JavaScript `import` is live binding for exports — reassignments in the exporting module visible to importers for `let`/`const` exports.

blocks.title: Interview one-liner
blocks.body: ES modules: strict, deferred, own scope, static imports. Classic scripts: sloppy default, global `var`, blocking unless defer/async. Node: CJS vs ESM interop is a deployment topic.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Parse HTML
items.body: Encounter `<script>` — classic scripts without `defer`/`async` block HTML parsing while downloading and executing.

items.title: Module scripts defer
items.body: `type="module"` downloads in parallel, executes after document parse, in order.

items.title: Resolve import graph
items.body: Engine fetches dependencies, instantiates module records, links exports to imports.

items.title: Evaluate modules
items.body: Run module bodies depth-first respecting cycles. Top-level await pauses that module's evaluation.

snippet.label: Module scope vs global script
snippet.explanation: Top-level `var` in modules creates a module binding, not a global. Classic scripts pollute the global object — a common migration footgun.

snippet.label: Static import hoisting
snippet.explanation: Import declarations are hoisted to the top of the module graph evaluation. The exporting module runs before importers use its bindings.

snippet.label: Node CJS vs ESM
snippet.explanation: Node treats `.cjs` as CommonJS and `.mjs` as ESM. Mixing `require` and `import` in one file is a syntax error — choose per package boundary.

snippet.label: Script loading attributes
snippet.code:
<!-- Blocks parsing, runs immediately -->
<script src="blocking.js"></script>

<!-- Downloads parallel, runs after HTML parsed -->
<script defer src="deferred.js"></script>

<!-- Module: defer by default, strict, CORS for cross-origin -->
<script type="module" src="app.mjs"></script>
snippet.explanation: `async` classic scripts run when ready (order not guaranteed). Module scripts behave like `defer` — predictable order for dependency graphs.

rows: Compiles to JS modules or CJS

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Using `var` in a module and expecting a global — it is module-scoped. `require` in an ESM file or `import` in CJS without dynamic `import()`. Forgetting CORS on cross-origin `<script type="module">`. Assuming bundler dev server behavior matches Node native ESM in production. Equating C# `using` with JS `import` — only JavaScript `import` executes the dependency.

interviewTakeaways: ES modules: strict, deferred, isolated scope, static `import`/`export`, live bindings.
Classic scripts: global `var`, sloppy default, blocking parse unless defer/async.
Node: `.mjs` / package `"type":"module"` for ESM; CJS uses `require` — interop needs care.
60s: Modules strict and scoped. Scripts can pollute global. import hoists and runs dependencies. C# using is not import. Bundlers flatten; Node prod follows spec.
Follow-up: what happens with circular ESM imports at evaluation time?
commonPitfalls: Expecting top-level var in a module to attach to window — it does not.
Mixing require and import in the same Node file without dynamic import().
Strong answer: 'ESM strict, deferred, module scope. CJS synchronous require. import executes; C# using does not load.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: C# `using` shortens type names at compile time. JavaScript `import` loads and evaluates the module graph. Assembly references in .csproj are closer to package.json dependencies.
TypeScript `module` and `moduleResolution` settings determine whether output is ESM or CommonJS. Types erase; load semantics follow emitted format.
